newsitem.title: UK: British hunt workers unite to fight ban threat.
newsitem.headline: British hunt workers unite to fight ban threat.

text.p: British huntsmen, gamekeepers and other country sports workers formed a trade union on Wednesday to fight any attempt to ban hunting if the opposition Labour Party wins the May 1 general election.
The Union of Country Sports Workers said 90,000 full-time jobs could be lost if fox and hare hunting were banned and this figure could rise to 160,000 if part-time workers were included.
The union fears that Labour, hot favourite to win the election, would ban hunting to hounds and that this would threaten shooting, fishing and other blood sports.
Labour has promised to allow a vote in parliament on whether hunting should be banned.

Field sports enthusiasts feel that many Labour members of parliament object to their pastimes on class grounds. Country people are quick to point out that hunting, shooting and fishing are enjoyed by people from all walks of life.

They say a ban on fox hunting would bring an end to one of the British countryside's most traditional and colourful sights -- a pack of hounds in full cry after a fox with the hunt on horseback in hot pursuit.
"Any political party which bans country sports will be scarred in rural areas for ever," said the union's chairman John Fretwell, who is huntsman of the Stowe beagles.

"They will be knee-deep in dishonour, knowing that they have made thousands of people homeless and jobless. They will be alienated from the countryside for generations," he told a news conference called to launch the union.
Flanked by his committee -- the huntsmen in traditional red coats and the gamekeepers in their tweeds -- Fretwell said those whose jobs were under threat were amongst Britain's lowest paid.

They included grooms, ghillies, foresters, saddlers, farriers, feed merchants and shopkeepers, all part of an industry that had a turnover of more than 6.2 billion pounds ($10.18 billion) a year, Fretwell said.
"We are doing it because we are dedicated to the sport," Fretwell said. "All workers in country sports want is to be left alone, We are not political animals."

With a hoped-for membership of 10,000 in its first six months, the union's main aims would be to lobby parliament and to protect members' interests from political threats. Early talks were planned with Labour leader Tony Blair and Conservative Prime Minister John Major.

Moves to ban handguns following last year's massacre of 16 children and their teacher at Dunblane primary school in Scotland had also increased the mood of nervousness among game shooters although shotguns were not an immediate target of legislation.
Fretwell said that animal rights lobbyists opposed to fox hunting had mounted a slicker public relations operation and it was now time for his members to make their voices heard.
"We are the silent majority. We should have our say," he said. ($1=.6088 Pound)
